goals.en:
Upon the successful completion of this course, students will be able to:
- Understand the contested nature of ethics 
- Distinguish between descriptive and normative questions
- Distinguish between meta-ethics, normative ethics, and applied ethics 
- Gain some insights from non-Western ethical traditions 
- Identify, analyse and explain some key ethical theories
- Formulate objections against each one of them 
- Apply ethical questions and reasoning to specific fields (in particular, public discourse ethics, feminist ethics, disability studies, environmental ethics, postcolonial studies)
- Identify relevant arguments and pick out flawed reasoning, in line with critical thinking skills
- Take seriously others’ perspectives when arguing for a case and treat persons with respect
- Formulate original arguments 
- Collaborate with peers to find arguments and objections on a given question

description.en: Have you ever wondered what’s wrong, if anything, with the herd immunity strategy to handle the global pandemic? How to repair historical injustices inflicted on colonised countries? What do we owe to people living with severe disabilities? The ethics course will tackle these questions and many more, related to the ethical norms that ought to govern our collective life. Students will be introduced to major ethical theories and challenged with thorny ethical dilemmas. Together we will discuss a wide range of topics, from animal rights, queer politics, privacy and security to post-colonialism. We will do so by listening to thinkers from various backgrounds and by arguing with each other. Spoiler alert: philosophy rarely gives definite answers, but triggers more and more questions. Philosophy can thus make us feel, at times, lost and confused. Yet novel questions are essential to expand our moral imagination. Moral imagination—the ability to envisage different moral perspectives, to invent new vocabulary and slogans (e.g. #MeToo), to picture what a fairer world would be—is essential to collective life. Without moral imagination, we would not be able to think of all of us human beings as equal. We would not be able to conceive of “non-human animals” as right holders. Without moral imagination, women would not have conceived of themselves as voters and slaves as worthy of freedom. Reading ancient and contemporary thinkers, scrutinising our moral intuitions, challenging our preconceptions and learning from others’ points of view are all ways to improve our ethical literacy. We thus invite you to a short, but intense, philosophical journey during which we will probably get a bit lost and confused at times, but we might also be able, if we stick together as a team, to find new, perhaps unexplored, moral paths.
